title: Literacy Educators: Let’s Get Serious about Noncognitive Skills
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that research-based literacy instruction must include a serious, strategic treatment of noncognitive skill development, and that aiming only at the Common Core's cognitive goals breeds frustration for teachers and students. Drawing on Paul Tough's How Children Succeed and James Heckman's work, he defines noncognitive skills as learnable habits, such as grit and self-control, that predict success but are not measured by intelligence metrics. His diagnosis is that most teachers care about these skills but lack a systematic, simplified list of which ones matter, largely because high-stakes testing rewards only cognitive gains. He surveys four such lists (Jim Burke's Academic Essentials, KIPP's character strengths, David Conley's ownership-of-learning skills, and NCTE's habits of mind) and explains why his academy has kept KIPP's seven strengths: simplicity, observable behavioural indicators, and a large community of practice. He then answers the objection that lists produce legalistic teaching by insisting they be treated as descriptive rather than prescriptive, and by arguing, against Penny Kittle, that great teaching needs both relationships and systems. He closes by calling for a shared professional language so that noncognitive skills enter the literacy conversation explicitly.
points: Stuart's core claim: literacy instruction aimed solely at the Common Core's cognitive goals will leave a vague frustration in the classroom unless noncognitive skills are taught strategically.
He traces teachers' lack of systematic noncognitive lists to decades of test-driven emphasis on cognitive skills, where there is no test for grit or self-control.

KIPP's seven character strengths are defended on three grounds: simple enough to grasp quickly, broken into observable behavioural indicators that resist buzzwordification, and shared by a large community of teachers.
He insists such lists be used descriptively, as a common language for the 'literacy plus what else' question, and warns that boxed-up prescriptive curricula would kill them.
Against Penny Kittle's claim that good teaching rests on relationships rather than systems, he argues a profession needs both to spread great teaching widely.
quotes: However, here’s the claim I’ll spend this post supporting (I've pawed around in the dark at it elsewhere, but that was quite a few months ago, and I've done more thinking in the interim): if you aim at the Common Core's goals (which are cognitive) and nothing else, you and/or a large amount of your students will begin to hate you and/or their life. A vague sense of frustration will live in your classroom, and you won't be able to put your finger on it.

Noncognitive skills are those things that aren't measured on traditional intelligence metrics (e.g., IQ) but are nonetheless being shown in study after study to significantly predict whether or not you’ll be successful. By calling them skills, I'm saying that, just like dribbling a soccer ball or writing your name or factoring an equation or reading closely, noncognitive skills can be intentionally taught and intentionally practiced and intentionally mastered.

But I would also argue that most teachers lack a systematic, simplified list of what noncognitive skills matter for their students' long-term flourishing. As a result, their attempts to instill noncognitive skills in their students are inefficient at least and, unfortunately, often largely ineffective.

But I would argue that anything that's got a shot of really having an impact in education should be complex enough to explore creatively for years and yet simplifiable enough to understand, in some fashion, in as little as an hour. We need simplified literacy instruction frameworks like the non-freaked out approach if we're to see kids getting more and better literacy instruction throughout their school day in all their classes.

The problem with the claim, though, is that I think we need relationships and systems to maximize the impact of our teaching, especially if great teaching is going to spread as far as it can go. Professions have frameworks and systems for describing best practices, and ours is a profession.

To get us back to our topic, the key, I think, lies in viewing systematic noncognitive skill lists as descriptive rather than prescriptive. Jim's list is a description of what proficient students can do. The KIPP list is a description of a set of habits that increase the likelihood of positive life outcomes.

But here's the gist — the literacy instruction conversation needs to include the noncognitive skill conversation, and we need to move forward with agreed upon language for referring to what skills matter most so that we, as a community of professionals, can get to the much more exciting work of exploring how in the world we get kids developing these highly predictive, literacy-enhancing skills.
